output.summary:
Advisory interpretation of one immutable LT Verdict analysis (analysis_id ff2a9752b81138f897422b4167ef5a67f5769e579320a62903676f78ea671ef9, run_id jmeter_jtl_csv-b87363cf1d89c0789e174268c6d25cd65abd36f7b623d4ea84fe253ceaabf1e7). The deterministic result is preserved exactly and is not altered by this advice: run_validity = VALID, policy_verdict = PASS, analysis_coverage = COMPLETE with no reasons, findings list empty.

The referenced PASS rests on exactly one policy check: rule_id "overall-errors", metric error_rate_ratio, operator lte, threshold 0.01, observed numerator 0 over denominator 2623 on the overall scope, status PASS. It therefore attests only that no recorded sample in the overall window was counted as an error. Latency and throughput were measured but no referenced rule judges them: overall latency_ms p50 11, p95 46, p99 77, max 904 across sample_count 2623; six JMETER_SAMPLER transactions ("add product to cart", "cart", "checkout", "home", "product", "reset cart") with 437-438 samples each and per-transaction maxima of 78, 187, 444, 904, 108 and 75 ms respectively. The overall maximum of 904 ms matches the "home" transaction maximum.

Nothing in this evidence supports stronger conclusions. Zero errors, an empty findings list, and COMPLETE analysis coverage do not establish stability, low load, absence of a problem, or spare capacity; no capacity bound, stage, load-ramp, time-series, generator resource guard, clock-synchronisation, or anomaly-detector data is referenced, and no NO_POLICY entry appears either (absence of a capacity entry is not a pass). Several tails are steep relative to their p95 on only 437-438 samples per transaction, so upper percentiles rest on very few observations. throughput_rps is given only as numerator/denominator pairs whose units and window are not defined in the referenced evidence, so those ratios must not be re-read as durations.

All advice below is limited to actions a test operator can perform: inspect the recorded data, verify clocks, configure policy, or rerun.

hypotheses.observation: The evidence contains a single policy_check (ref analysis-result.json#/evidence/7): rule_id "overall-errors", metric error_rate_ratio, operator lte, threshold 0.01, observed 0/2623, status PASS, tied to metric_evidence_id "metric-summary-overall". The facts record policy_verdict PASS. Latency and throughput metric summaries are present for the overall scope and for six transactions, but no policy_check references latency_ms or throughput_rps.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The policy set configured for this run may define only an error-rate rule, so the PASS verdict expresses an error-rate judgement alone while the latency and throughput measurements remain unjudged. It is also possible that latency or throughput rules exist but were not included in this evidence set; the referenced data cannot distinguish these.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the policy configuration used for this analysis and enumerate the rules that were evaluated (confirm whether rule_id "overall-errors" is the only one). If latency or throughput rules were intended, add them with explicit thresholds and re-run the analysis; if they were deliberately omitted, record that the PASS covers error rate only.

hypotheses.observation: Overall latency_ms is p50 11, p95 46, p99 77, max 904 (sample_count 2623). Among the six transaction summaries, only "home" reports max 904 ms, with p50 27, p95 61, p99 96 and sample_count 438. The next largest transaction maximum is 444 ms ("checkout").
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The overall maximum appears to be carried by the "home" transaction, whose whole distribution sits above the other transactions (p50 27 ms versus 3-13 ms elsewhere). A single extreme value far above that transaction's own p99 of 96 ms could be an isolated outlier, a first-sample or warm-up effect, or a genuine slow response; the referenced evidence contains no timestamps, no time series and no per-sample rows, so it cannot separate these.
hypotheses.recommended_check: First verify the clock relationship between the JMeter generator host and the system under test, since none is evidenced here. Then inspect the raw JTL rows for the "home" label sorted by elapsed time, and look at where the slowest samples fall relative to the start of the run and whether they are isolated or clustered.

hypotheses.observation: Per-transaction sample counts are small and near-identical: 437 for "add product to cart", "cart", "checkout", "product" and "reset cart", and 438 for "home". Several distributions are steep in the upper tail relative to their p95, e.g. "reset cart" p95 7 ms versus p99 47 ms and max 75 ms, and "add product to cart" p50 3 ms, p95 30 ms, p99 72 ms, max 78 ms.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: With roughly 437 samples per transaction, one percent of the distribution corresponds to only a handful of observations, so p99 and max are estimated from very few rows and are sensitive to individual slow samples. The steep p95-to-p99 gaps may therefore reflect sparse sampling of the tail rather than a sustained latency regime; alternatively they may reflect real intermittent slowness. The referenced summaries alone cannot tell which.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the per-sample elapsed-time values for "reset cart" and "add product to cart" (histogram or the individual slowest rows) rather than relying on the percentile alone. If tail percentiles are to drive decisions, plan a longer or repeated run at the same load to raise the per-transaction sample count, and treat it as a separate run rather than a continuation of this one.

hypotheses.observation: error_count is 0 and the error_rate_ratio numerator is 0 for the overall scope (0/2623) and for every one of the six transaction scopes (0/437 or 0/438). The single policy check on error_rate_ratio against threshold 0.01 returned PASS.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The zero error count is consistent with a run in which no sample failed. It is equally consistent with failures not being recorded or classified as errors in the JTL - for example missing or disabled assertions, or non-successful responses still flagged successful - because the referenced evidence carries only aggregate counts and no response codes, assertion results, or failure messages.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the JTL success/failure column and the response-code and failure-message columns for a sample of rows, and confirm the assertion configuration in the JMeter test plan. If assertions are absent or permissive, add them and rerun before relying on the error-rate PASS.

hypotheses.observation: throughput_rps is reported only as numerator/denominator pairs. The overall scope is 2623000/44986, and every transaction scope reuses the same denominator 44986 with numerators 437000 (438000 for "home").
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The identical denominator across overall and per-transaction scopes suggests one shared elapsed window applied to all scopes, so per-transaction rates would be expressed over the whole run window rather than over each transaction's active time. The units of the numerator and denominator and the definition of the window are not stated anywhere in the referenced evidence, so any conversion to requests per second - or any reading of 44986 as a duration - would be an unsupported inference.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the evidence schema or analysis configuration that defines throughput_rps numerator and denominator units and the window used, and compare that window against the first and last timestamps recorded in the JTL. Do not compare these ratios with counts from a different scope or window.

hypotheses.observation: The six per-transaction sample counts (437, 437, 437, 438, 437, 437) add to 2623, which equals the overall sample_count of 2623. All six transaction scopes carry sample_kind JMETER_SAMPLER and an empty group_path.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: This arithmetic equality is consistent with every recorded sample mapping to exactly one of the six reported transaction labels, with no samples outside them. It is not proof: overall and per-transaction counts are different scopes, and equality of totals does not establish that the same rows or the same window underlie both. The equality could also be coincidental if some rows were excluded from one scope and not the other.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect the distinct label values present in the JTL and their row counts, and confirm which rows are included in the overall scope versus the transaction scopes (including any sub-sample or controller rows excluded from the transaction view).

hypotheses.observation: The facts state run_validity VALID and analysis_coverage COMPLETE with an empty reasons array, and the findings array is empty. The evidence set contains seven metric summaries and one policy check only - no capacity, stage, load-ramp, time-series, generator resource guard, clock, or anomaly-detector entries are referenced.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: An empty findings list alongside COMPLETE coverage means the analyses that were run produced no findings; it does not mean the system is stable, lightly loaded, or has spare capacity, and COMPLETE coverage describes the analysis performed rather than the breadth of policy evaluated. Because no detector or time-series data is referenced here, no statement about the presence, count, or sensitivity of anomaly testing can be made from this evidence.

If load-level or capacity behaviour matters, plan a staged rerun with verified product outcomes per stage; a capacity bound comes from such stages, and no knee-based reading is available.
